Price Spreads Commission
the afternoon papers in some parts of Canada and is in most of the morning papers of today. I have a copy of one paper under my hand in which five or six columns are devoted to the final report of the commission. I am not complaining with respect to the attitude of the press; it is the business of the press to get ail the information it can, but after what has been said in this house with respect to preserving the privileges of this parliament, not only on this side but by hon. gentlemen opposite as well, it certainly would appear that the giving out of what is published here is, on the part of someone, in the nature of an act of contempt alike of parliament and of the government. I think the government had better appoint a commission to inquire into what member of this commission, if any, or what person connected with it is responsible for giving this information to the press before either the government or parliament have received it.
I should like to suggest also that when the government are considering the legislation that is to be based upon the recommendations of this commission, with respect to unfair practices and unethical proceedings, it might consider whether it is not possible to enact some legislation which will prevent unfair practices and unethical proceedings on the part of chairmen of committees of this House of Commons when dealing with price spreads and mass-buying, and on the part of some member or members of royal commissions when they are dealing with the same subjects. This is a matter that should not be allowed to pass lightly; it is a matter that concerns the government and all hon. members of this house. I submit that parliamentary government can only be carried on if we observe the rules of parliament, and judicial and quasi-judicial bodies can only be upheld if judicial procedure is followed. The rules and practices both of parliament and judicial bodies have been violated by someone who has had a pretty intimate association with the committee and also with the commission. I hope the government will take up this matter seriously, in order to preserve the privileges of this house and the rights of all parties with respect to matters of this kind.

unnecessarily to prolong the observations I began last evening. May I state briefly that I oppose the long adjournment because I do not want the business of the country to be delayed. On this occasion I do not wish to be accused of delaying the business of the house by making a long speech.
Last night I was discussing one of the reasons given by the government in favour of a long adjournment, namely, the considerable time required for the preparation of legislation to implement the recommendations of the royal commission on price spreads and mass buying. I said last night, and now repeat, that if the government does not know the recommendations of the commission they are the only ones who have not that information, because for days, weeks, and 
months the newspapers throughout the country have published columns concerning those recommendations.
The report of the commission was signed at eleven o'clock this morning and should be presented to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to-day. Yet, last evening's newspapers and again the newspapers on the streets this morning contained columns about the recommendations of the commission, and quoted verbatim whole sections of the report. Therefore the government surely will not profess ignorance of at least a general idea of the report. Now the report has been signed and will be presented. The legislation suggested by the commission is expressed in great detail in the report, and full and complete indications are given of the type of legislation the commission desires. Therefore very little time should be necessary for the government to draft bills arising out of the recommendations. As the first member of the commission to speak, after the presentation of the report, it is only fitting that there should be a tribute of appreciation to the secretary of the commission, Mr. L. B. Pearson, of the Department of External Affairs, who was loaned to us. We cannot be too grateful for the assistance and help received from him. What I say about Mr. Pearson I would say, too, about his assistants, Mr. W. J. Cooper and Professor C. A. Curtis, and the other competent and expert economists who have assisted us throughout the investigation.
Only a few moments ago I listened to the observations of the right hon. leader of the opposition regarding the leakage of the report of the commission. It is not necessary for me to state that this unfortunate leakage has not been due to any action of any Liberal member of the commission.

Although the present Prime Minister of Canada said in the election of 1930, "Farmers of Canada, we will make tariffs fight for you," the tariffs have been used in the last five years, not to fight for the farmers, but to fight against them. Immediately after the election, at the special session of 1930, the tariffs were raised against the farmers and on account of that raise in the tariffs the farmers had to pay more for their farm implements, more for their cream separators, more for their gasoline motors and for many other articles which they have to buy. They had to pay more for everything they had to buy, and at the same time they received less for their butter and for all the products they had to sell.
But that was not sufficient. At the general session of 1932 the tariffs were raised again against the farmers. Then we had the imperial conference in 1932, and following that, occasion was taken again to raise the tariffs against the farmers and to restrict the markets and the outlets for the produce of the farm. Therefore I am not surprised, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers are anxious to meet this government and to settle accounts with them. The farmers of Canada want an election right now, even though some few young people may not have their names on the list.
It would not be such a bad thing for the farmers if there was not a revision of the lists at all. This revision is going to cost quite a pile of money, too much money. The printing of the lists themselves has cost a lot of money, and I understand that the printing and the revision of the lists is going to cost over a million dollars, an expense that is absolutely unnecessary. The old system was a good one, and there was no demand for a change. It was working to perfection, and there was no complaint against it. Under the old system the lists were made on the eve of an election by the electoral officer and the returning officers all over Canada, and it did not cost much money. One of the advantages of that system was that if an elector's name had been omitted from the list he could vote if qualified on being identified at the poll by someone who knew him. But under the present system a lot of unnecessary officials have been appointed and a lot of money has been spent unnecessarily, and there is the danger of names being misspelled or misinscribed on the list, and danger also of names being omitted altogether, and that has occurred in every county of the province of Quebec. Many names have been misspelled and wrongly inscribed on the lists. The farmers

The people have been taxed almost beyond their capacity to pay taxation, and the farmers of Canada do not want to pay any further taxation. They want no more public money spent uselessly. I do not think that even the illness of the Prime Minister warrants delay at this late stage in the life of this parliament. We have seen almost every promise made by this government broken, and we have seen the futility of the legislation they have brought down. That legislation has not in any single instance effected a cure or brought about any relief in the situation that now exists. Take the statement which has been made by my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger). We were told that by an increase in tariffs unemployment would be ended in Canada; the electors of the country were given that assurance. The Liberal opposition in the House of Commons have remained quiescent; they have given this government every chance in the world, they have subscribed to any -particular legislation that seemed to be in the interests of the people, though the opposition have warned the government of course on all occasions that the legislation would be without effect. And has not our word been amply proven? What is the state of employment to-day? Has there been any relief to the unemployment situation 
in the last three or four years? For two or three years we have been hearing that business was on the upgrade, prosperity being just around the corner, but statements of that kind are no longer being made by members of the government. It has -been conceded not only by business men but -by economists that the root of all evil of the trouble lies in the fa-ct that this government have placed barriers against trade and restricted trade on every occasion; hence the position in which we find ourselves to-day. Year after year we have had deficits and additional taxation, and year after year individuals engaged in the basic industries of the country, with the exception of gold mining and the production of nickel, have found themselves in the unfortunate position of being less able to pay their taxes than in previous years. What is the situation today? Unless there is a- right about face in Canada, we shall not be able to pay the taxes imposed on us. Worse than that, the effect of this legislation has spread to the provinces, for the provincial governments are facing difficulties right and left. Take the financial statement of any of the provinces; does it make pleasant reading? Have we a feeling that we are making progress, or do we not rather feel that we are going backward? Every one of the provinces has to announce deficit after deficit with an addition to its debt. Need I tell you. Mr. Speaker, that t-here can be only one end to this sort of thing? In a private business it does not matter who finds himself in this unfortunate position, he must sooner or later succumb and have the sheriff take control.
The government of the day have made much of the fact that they have preserved the credit of Canada and have been able to pay their way. Well, they have been able to pay their way by further borrowing; that is the only way. Then they -take much credit for the fact that they have had favourable balances of trade. How are favourable balances of trade secured? When they took office the trade of the country was nearly two and a quarter billions, and what is it to-day? It has gradually decreased until it averages a little over one billion, and by the reduction in trade, by restriction of imports into the country and partly by the empire agreements, regarding which I shall have a word or two to say, they have been able to show a favourable balance of trade. But they have done so at the expense of the people of Canada; there is a heavier burden of taxation on the people's shoulder's, added to every session of parliament, and that condition would continue -were hon. gentlemen permitted to hold another session.

My hon. friends do not seem to realize that there must be, as I say, a right about face in the policy of the government before the people can secure any relief. That does not seem to occur to them. No; we have nothing but procrastination in dealing with these matters. My hon. friends have imbibed the spirit of nationalism from other countries despite the fact other countries are in as difficult a situation. They follow these other countries; there is no originality about their proposals for relief. All we are told is .that their social legislation will meet the difficulties of the situation. Will anyone tell me how unemployment insurance will benefit the situation? I have not yet discovered anyone who wants it as we have it under the present act. How will the shortening of hours of labour and the minimum wage improve matters? An amusing thing gleaned from the report this afternoon, which one reporter seems to have got hold of in some way, is the statement that they are not recommending a forty-eight hour week but one of forty-four hours. Again, the government of the day find themselves in the unfortunate position of having to make changes in that respect. I suppose this is the reason: They want to have some relief, some time to get their second wind, to see whether they cannot think up some new idea that will catch the popular fancy.
I was greatly amused yesterday listening to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) when he made a statement as to when the election would be. He said dispassionately to this house that they would have an election when they thought they could win. If we have to wait until this government think they can win, we may as well all go home and go to work and wait another five years.

Let us turn to the legislation for unemployment insurance. In my opinion, sir, that measure does not go far enough. I am of the opinion it should include many workers who, as the Prime Minister pointed out, are very seldom unemployed. If we are to apply the law of averages I say the legislation should be extended to include workers employed in banks, in insurance offices and in other vocations,-workers who are not now included. I can remember that in 1930 the statement was made during the campaign that if elected the 'Conservative party would take care of the unemployed. Under normal conditions in Canada the vast majority of people now employed will, undoubtedly, continue to be employed. Consequently while these employed persons have no objection to bearing their fair share of the costs they feel the privilege should be extended so that the law of averages should apply. My view is that the scheme would be more effective if it were extended to include more than it does at the present time.
If I remember correctly, during the campaign of 1930, speaking in the maritimes, the present Prime Minister expressed a great deal of sympathy for the railway employees. The government has undertaken the setting of minimum wages. Labour organizations in Canada have always contended that they do not want minimum wage legislation, because employers invariably have construed minimum wage measures as measures setting maximum wages. However, conditions have changed and the government has seen fit to introduce such legislation. There is one principle which I think should be followed in connection with that matter. It could not very well be worked out when it was a question of private negotiation between labour organizations and employers, but it should be possible to work it out now. A man with a family should most certainly receive more money for his labour than a man who has no

Our leader and the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) were equally sure that it was not. That notice of motion by the Hon. Mr. Price reads as follows:

Canada, with 520.221 hundredweight of cheese out of a total of 2,988,567 hundredweight, is now relatively an unimportant factor in this trade in which at one time she was preeminent.
Since the Ottawa agreements have been signed, British imports of Canadian oheese have dropped from year to year. Here is an official government publication declaring, in March, 1935, that Canada is in a poor position in respect of cheese exports.
While our exports were dwindling, Australia and New Zealand, who signed the Ottawa agreements, were shipping far greater quantities of their cheese; that is to say, while our exports were reduced, the exports from those two countries were reaching a considerably higher figure, to the prejudice of our own farmers. In 1931, England imported 1,732,000 cwt. from New Zealand; in 1933, 2,059,393 cwt. and, in the eleven months ending November 30, 1934, New Zealand shipped 1,973,703 cwt. Australian exports are also greater. I submit respectfully, sir, that, instead of asking for an adjournment of the house, the government would be well advised to review the Ottawa

agreements in order to put our cheese factories in the same favourable position as they were before the conclusion of those agreements.
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger), in his splendid speech this afternoon, reminded us that one of the chief causes of the miserable situation in which the Canadian farmer finds himself to-day might be found in the fact that our farmers are selling their products at a low figure, while they have to pay high prices for the manufactured goods they have to buy.
Farmers in my constituency-and those of Quebec generally-have signed a petition addressed to the Prime Minister of this Dominion asking the government to fix a minimum price on a number of products and establish an export premium on butter and cheese. As this petition is of great importance, perhaps the house will allow me to quote it. Having described the pitiful condition of our farmers, they were asking the government, in January last, to fix-
... a minimum price as follows on the following products: butter, thirty cents per pound; cheese, fifteen cents per pound; eggs, twenty-five cents per dozen; pork, ten cents per pound; potatoes, fifty cents per bag.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers who signed this petition are very moderate in their claims.
They ask, in the second place, for an export bonus on cheese as well' as on butter. Their petition continues:
The undersigned believe that with such a minimum price and such an export bonus, the agricultural situation, which forms the basis of our economic system, would very appreciably improve and that, as a result, the general business situation of the country would benefit to a great extent.
There is at present a minimum price on wheat; this government has already granted a bonus of 5 cents a bushel on wheat exports, and the right hon. the Prime Minister has moreover announced a bill to reduce the hours of labour and one to establish a minimum wage. The legislation requested by the signers of this petition is somewhat similar to that which the Prime Minister has submitted to us. In order that such legislation may be effectual, it must necessarily apply to the whole country, as butter and cheese are produced in every province of Canada.
The ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in his letter of January 19, 1934, which was at the same time as his letter of resignation dated October 26, 1934, wrote to the Prime Minister as follows:
On your return from the International Economic Conference I submitted to you in writing, and discussed later with you in conversation, proposals regarding certain problems

in Canada, among them being the plight of the butter producer, and the necessity of action being taken before the winter months set in, to raise the price of butter to the producer,-
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister had this plan before him for over a year, but he did nothing about it. That is no doubt the reason why the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce added to his letter from which I have just quoted the following words:
-you will allow me to say most clearly that I fear you have permitted certain problems of a more or less international or general character to so obsess your mind and your attention that it has made it impossible for you to appreciate some of these pressing Canadian problems, which, while difficult of solution, are quite within the power of parliament.
If, as the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated-and he had been the Prime Minister's colleague during four years-international questions so obsessed the mind of the Prime Minister as to make him neglect purely Canadian questions, it is not surprising that he and his colleagues should not have had time to direct their thoughts towards improving agricultural conditions in this country.
I transmitted to the right hon. the Prime Minister petitions signed by a large number of farmers in my constituency, and I sincerely trust that the ministers from the province of Quebec will remind their chief of the promise he made in. 1930 to obtain for the farmer a higher price for his products and that they will urge him to grant the request contained in these petitions.	.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto East) moved the third reading of Bill No. 50, to amend the Post Office Act (newspaper ownership).

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Before this bill is read the third time I wish to say a few words regarding it, seeing that I had not an opportunity of joining in the discussion when it was previously before the house. I do not exactly desire to oppose the bill but rather to qualify the support I am willing to give it. There is nothing wrong in principle about it, but I am afraid it will not serve any great purpose. In the first place I regret that it proceds in an indirect way. I appreciate the fact that it might not have been possible to put through a bill covering this subject which would deal directly with it, but I have my doubts as to whether we might not safely have left the matter alone instead of proceeding with it as here proposed. It is a bill to amend the Post Office Act, though the purpose is to obtain a list of the shareholders, owners and others associated with every newspaper. As pointed out before in the discussion in committee- and I think it was also pointed out when a similar bill was before the house in previous sessions-there is no possible sanction for it, though the bill declares that if its provisions are not observed by any publication that publication shall be denied the privileges of the mail. This is an indirect and circuitous way of dealing with the matter, and it leaves in my mind a doubt whether this parliament could deal with it in a direct and more regular way. I admit that at the present time the privileges granted by the Post Office Department to large newspapers is so considerable, in the reduction of post office rates, that the sanction may work; but I wish to qualify that part of the bill. I do not think that this way of legislating on different matters should be greatly encouraged, even if in this instance it may seem to be the proper method of dealing with a situation that might not be met otherwise.
The main point I wish to make is that even if you succeed in obtaining a list of editors, publishers, shareholders and others connected with a newspaper-my hon. friend has tried to make it as complete as possible-I am not sure that this will finally achieve the purpose the hon. gentleman has in mind. A list of
Post Office Act-N ewspapers

the names of owners and especially shareholders of a large newspaper to-day will not necessarily disclose the motive that may be behind a particular attitude which that paper takes. A newspaper to-day is primarily a business concern and quite a number of persons invest their money in it, as in any other industrial enterprise, merely for possible profit. They are not necessarily interested in the attitude of the paper on a certain occasion towards a particular question.
In Montreal for a considerable time we had two English papers published in the evening, one giving the Conservative attitude and the other the Liberal, and yet it was well known that they belonged to the same man, the object of the so-called Liberal newspaper being merely to close the field of competition in order that the larger paper might have it all its own way. You may say that this is the very thing which this bill would prevent, inasmuch as it would compel the owner to disclose his identity and the fact that he owned both newspapers. But the fact is that everyone was aware of his ownership of these papers; it was common knowledge. Had a bill like this been in force then there is no doubt that he would have used other names so as to avoid disclosing his ownership of one of the papers. A bill such as this might have operated in the opposite direction to that which the hon. gentleman desires.
I would point out further that newspapers are the year round primarily purveyors of information. The old party paper which used to give only one side has pretty well disappeared; to-day a newspaper of a certain standing gives information on both sides. I do not overlook the fact that we have very strong party newspapers which, through their editorials, espouse a political cause and certainly exert an influence in that field. But even such newspapers, if they wish to retain their standing in newspaperdom, must convey information to the people; they must give information on both sides of the question-or may I say, in deference to my hon. friends in the corner, on all three sides of the question. With respect to a party paper of that description, supporting one or other political group, it is not very material that you should know who precisely is the man or who are the men giving it financial support. You know that it is Liberal or that it is Conservative. But the larger newspaper-and we have quite a number of them to-day-is not

devoted strictly to one or other of the political parties; it is a business concern, a purveyor of information; it disseminates information in all directions, gathering it from all sources, and its pages are read, if it is a so-called Conservative paper, by Liberal readers, and vice versa if it is supposed to be a liberal journal. And it is read by those belonging to the third party. But the main object of such newspapers is, I repeat, not political; it is a business proposition. And when these newspapers attain a certain degree of efficiency as carriers of news they also become a medium for advertising. Here again it is merely an industrial concern. I do not'think there is any need to get a list of all the people interested in a newspaper carrying advertisements or printing news in that way, any more than there would be such a need with regard to any other industrial enterprise. For that reason, it seems to me that even if this bill is adopted it will not serve the purpose its promoter has in mind.
Judging by his own commentaries, the object the sponsor of the bill seeks to attain is to find out who is the sinister influence behind a certain attitude on the part of a newspaper towards a particular question, or who is the political fiend that has inspired a certain comment on a certain bill. I do not think you will obtain that information by getting a list of the shareholders of newspapers, for the reasons I have given. I repeat, most of the shareholders are interested in the paper for business reasons; they are anxious to see the paper maintain its circulation by disseminating news to as large a number of subscribers as possible, and they want it to get as many advertisements as it can. If at a particular moment in the life of a newspaper -I am not speaking of the party newspaper but of the large journals-it appears to support a particular party in the first part of the year and another party in the latter part of the year, then I do not think that by obtaining a list of the shareholders you will find out the reason for these changes in the newspaper's atmosphere. If that sort of paper wishes to carry special propaganda, those who are really interested will carefully hide behind fictitious names; they will take care not to disclose their identity. This list, prepared with great care and submitted to my genial friend the Postmaster General, will not disclose the purpose behind it.
I read in subsection 2 that it is also proposed to have all reading or editorial matter for the publication of which money is paid or valuable consideration given plainly marked

Post Office Act-Newspapers
"advertisement." That also reads very well, but what does it mean? It means that if editorial matter is directly paid for by someone who wants it published, it will be marked "advertisement," but anyone with a little experience in newspapers knows that is not the way it is done. A financial institution or industrial concern will give an advertisement to a newspaper and will pay for it at so much per line. Then they will submit besides some reading matter which they suggest it would be desirable for the paper to publish, but they do not pay for it. It is not likely the reading matter would be published if the advertisement were not published, but in the long run when a paper has a client of that description there is no money paid directly for the publication of such reading matter. There again you will catch the small fish but miss the larger one. If a man wants a little bit of reading matter printed to serve a special purpose and pays for it, you reach him, but a large concern that has a contract for a year with a newspaper, and there is an understanding that these men, being good clients, should be treated liberally, reading matter will be printed in the paper for which they do not pay. That will not come under this section at all; yet there is no doubt that it is advertising in the same sense as the smaller ones I have just referred to.
From these remarks it would appear that I am not very strongly in favour of the bill. But I do not desire to oppose it. I do not think it is going to be very useful, but at the same time I believe it is harmless. I have no objection to the list of shareholders of a newspaper being known to the public. But from my experience as a newspaper man I wish to warn the public against attaching too much importance to such a bill, or concluding from the publication of such names that those people and those only are responsible for whatever the newspaper publishes. In short, this bill is very much like some of the reforms of the government; it is good in principle but it is not going to accomplish very much in practice.

While I am quite in favour of this bill, I take this opportunity, now that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is here, of asking if he would be good enough to give his view. I draw his attention to subsection 2, which I submit conflicts with the jurisdiction of the provinces over property and civil rights. In the first place this is an act to amend the Post Office Act, but subsection 2 has no reference to the Post Office Act in any way, shape or form. This subsection
requires that any matter published for which money or other valuable consideration is given shall be marked "advertisement", and for failure to comply with this requirement a fine of not less than $50 and not more than $500 is provided. That is a peculiar provision to put under the Post Office Act. As I said the other night, a similar bill was put through this house some years ago and was thrown out in the other chamber for the reason that it conflicted with the rights of the provinces.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
With reference to the objections taken in the house last Friday night to this bill and the question of jurisdiction raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), under the British North America Act the regulation of the post office is under federal jurisdiction. Subsection 2, to which the hon. gentleman referred, is simply a regulation for the post office. The Postmaster General can refuse admission to the mails of any newspaper in Canada and need not give any reason for doing so. For that reason the section is intra vires of this parliament. It does not in any sense relate to property and civil rights.
With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), who supports the bill, I entirely agree with his comments about certain scurrilous publications. They are not newspapers; they do not conform to the law of libel and slander; they show np editor or office of publication, and parliament should in some way control that type of scurrilous circular. They do not come under the provisions of the Post Office Act; they are under the authority of the chief electoral officer under the new election act, and it is his duty to see that this class of literature is prohibited. It is contrary to both the Dominion Elections Act and the criminal code as well as the law of libel and slander, which is provincial. If the hon. gentleman will draft an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act to take care of circulars and dodgers of this kind used at election time, commonly known as roorbacks, I will second it. Such publications do not come under this
2572	COMMONS
Long Adjournment-Mr. MacMillan (Mackenzie)
bill or any act of the federal or provincial legislatures, because they are not newspapers.
Referring to the observations of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), he was a member of the administration that supported this bill for six years in this house. While he is not opposing the bill, he offered some criticisms of it; but I may tell him that this has been the law in England for many years and in the United States since 1912, and it has worked well. Why should any society, because it is incorporated under the newspaper law, be free from obligation to disclose any details regarding its business? This is a very moderate bill, providing for what has been found to be in the public interest. There never was a time in the history of this country, in view of the many important problems facing it, when it was more necessary that hon. members should speak out and demand publicity as to the owners of that small section of the press that would be opposed to this bill. I paid tribute the other night to what the press has done, and I need not say anything further on that. I believe this is good legislation. It was part of the Liberal platform of 1919. It originated with the Liberal party in Great Britain. This particular bill has been examined by the law officers and other lawyers, and is intra vires of this parliament.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PROLONGED ADJOURNMENT EXPRESSED IN AMENDMENT TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment which is now before the house is timely and imperative. There is no other way of regarding it. The conditions which prevail throughout the entire country demand our immediate and undivided attention. During the first and second weeks of this year the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) delivered a series of radio addresses, and by the statements he made therein set the country all agog. The old order, which has existed for many centuries, was to be obliterated, he said, and replaced by a new social order. This new social order has been advocated by and has been a part of the policy of the Liberal party for many years. When the house opened this year and the government
rMr. Church.]
undertook to place this reform legislation on the statute books, therefore, the official opposition rendered every assistance possible in order to facilitate the passing of these measures so they would become law and be put into operation in this country. Now we have the government coming forward with the proposal that we should have an adjournment of five or six weeks. Having regard to the conditions that prevail throughout the country I contend that this request is very unreasonable and savours of insincerity. There is not a political party in this house, or in the country so far as that goes, that is better equipped to put these reform measures into operation than the Liberal party, because the Liberal party is a party of action and reform.

speechtext:
I am glad that my statement meets with approval on the other side of the house as well as on this side. I hope it will not be considered that I am using	veiy strong	language when	Ideclare	that	the present	government	is	a
government of usurpers. This government came into office in August, 1930. Its popularity began its great and unparalleled retreat in 1932. In that year a by-election was held in the constituency of South Huron, and naturally it was expected, as is always expected, that a supporter of the government would be returned. It is only fair to the government to say that the seat was held by a Liberal prior to the by-election, but the important point to consider is that in the by-election a Liberal was elected by a greater majority than had been given the previous candidate in 1930. That was the first intimation to the government that their popularity was on the wane to a considerable extent.
Then in August, 1933, a provincial election was held in the banner province of Liberalism, Nova Scotia. A Conservative government dissolved the legislature, but after the election the Liberal party formed a government. Then there were three by-elections in different parts of Canada on October 23 of the same year. The constituency of Restigouche-Madawaska, which was represented by a Conservative prior to the by-election, returned a Liberal by such a handsome majority that the Conservative candidate contributed $200 to the general revenue of the Dominion of Canada. In the constituency of Yamaska a Liberal was returned with an increased majority, and in the constituency of Mackenzie a Liberal was elected wth a majority of 1,614. That was

Long Adjournment-Mr. MacMillan (Mackenzie)
the first time in twenty-one or twenty-two years that a Liberal candidate had been elected to represent that constituency. Then a provincial election was held in British Columbia; a Conservative government dissolved the legislature but when it reassembled after the general election a Liberal government was in office. That was a further indication to this government that they should seriously consider dissolving parliament and consulting the people.
On June 19, 1934, a terrible catastrophe-so far as the interests of the Conservative party were concerned-occurred in two widely separated parts of the dominion. In the province of Ontario a Conservative government dissolved the legislature, but after the election the Liberal party formed the government. In the province of Saskatchewan a Conservative government dissolved the legislature but after the election not a single Conservative was returned to tell the tale. Of fifty-five members returned fifty were Liberals and five belonged to the new party which is fast disappearing. Of those five only one was elected by a majority vote. We all remember the good old hymn:
Time like an ever rolling stream
Bears all its sons away-
Because of this there were three by-elections in the province of Ontario, and two other vacancies caused by the resignation of members. I am not going to mention the political complexions of those constituencies prior to the by-elections, which were held September 24, 1934, but as a result four Liberals and one very independent Conservative were returned. I submit that the day following those by-elections the government should have acquiesced in the logic of events, made an unconditional surrender and gone to the people. So in relating the political events of the Dominion of Canada in the last three years I am sure hon. members will agree that I did not use a very strong term when I said that this was a government of usurpers.
You know, Mr. Speaker, when rats know that the ship is sinking they drop their can openers and beat it by the short route. The ship of state of the Dominion of Canada has been bombarded from all sides for the last three years, but the captain and crew, instead of veering the vessel to port, made for the open sea. With regard to these by-elections to which I referred and the representatives returned to this House of Commons, in all humility I am going to make the statement that the most important and the biggest shot of all came from the con-92582-104
stituency of Mackenzie. My reason for making that statement is that that shot not only did untold harm to the ship of state; it also ricocheted and knocked the block clean off an unnatural enemy of the state.
Now, Mr. Speaker, having related the political events that have taken place in this dominion since 1932, let us come to the conditions which exist at the present time. I submit that the government must go further than they have gone in order to assist the people and alleviate the distress which exists in many parts of the country to-day. I am referring more particularly to western Canada, from which I come. Every part of the country is well represented in this house; each member can speak for the part he represents, but I am now speaking for the province of Saskatchewan, and the conditions that prevail in that province are the conditions that prevail in the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta. We have had a period of depression lasting for five years. The farmers, who form the basic industry of the three prairie provinces, have not been able to make ends meet. That has not been through any fault of the farmer or the toiler; it has been because conditions have prevailed over which they have had no control. We must remember that many enterprises in this country have made profits and declared dividends even during the period of depression. The chartered banks and other financial institutions have been declaring dividends since 1930. Of course they declared dividends prior to that time, but I am not going beyond 1930, when the depression began. Even in 1932, probably the poorest year in Canadian history, the chartered banks and financial institutions of this country declared dividends while the farmers were declaring losses. The farmers are not able to make ends meet; they cannot meet the obligations they incurred during days of prosperity. Something must be done to help those people, and I submit that before dissolution of parliament the government should do more than it has done in the past. I do not speak in any spirit of criticism, because undoubtedly the government has experienced difficulties since attaining office in 1930. I submit, however, that they could have done more than they have done. It is inevitable that the debts of the country are not going to be paid one hundred per cent. I believe I made the same statement when I spoke last year in the debate on the budget. What can be done? I submit the government could do something, and that it would not be necessary to add one cent to our public debt. When I make these

2574	COMMONS
Long Adjournment-Mr. MacMillan (Mackenzie)
observations I mean there must be an adjustment of debts.
The statement may be made that legislation was passed last year which would have the effect of helping people who are in debt and who wish to make settlements of those debts. The farmers throughout the country are an independent class of people, a condition which I believe is only natural when we realize that day in and day out they are communing with nature. They are men of honour; they are men with every desire to meet the obligations which they have incurred, and they do not ask reductions or anything else. However when those farmers are placed in a position where they cannot meet their obligations then I submit it behooves the government, and every person in a position to do so, to render assistance to those people by making it possible for them to meet their obligations.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have a platform. Of course their platform changes with every new moon, but since that party came into existence there is at least one plank they have always had, namely the statutory settlement of debts. I submit that is the only way to assist the farmers. Although giving the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) due credit for the legislation passed during the last session, I must say that when the farmer has to prostrate himself before his creditor, when he has to make an application to an official receiver in order to bring himself and his creditor together for the purpose of making satisfactory arrangements, he is placing himself in an undesirable position. Under conditions such as I have described, conditions over which the farmer has no control, there should be a statutory declaration on the compromise of debts, and debts should be classified. That is the only way in which settlements can be properly made, namely by statutory regulation.
Speaking of the classification of debts, may I illustrate by some further observations. There is an old saying that every tub must stand on its own bottom. Let us consider the man who has borrowed $1,000 in cash and given security by way of a mortgage on his homestead. I say that $1,000 should be paid. Some arrangements should be made with regard to interest. I will go farther and say that since the year 1930 any man who has been able to pay interest on his indebtedness 

and if he has done that he has done well- a portion of that interest should be credited by compromising on the interest and reducing it to a rate not higher than five per cent. On the other hand if a man sells me a quarter section of land, and by selling me that quarter section makes a profit of $1,500, then I say 
that not only should the interest be adjusted but the profit he made on that transaction should be compromised as well. I use that illustration so that hon. members will understand what I mean, namely that the debts should be classified.
I am not going to say any more about debts: possibly all of us talk too much about them. May I now come to another matter which in my view is of extreme importance to the people of Canada, namely the reform measures, some of which have already been introduced by the government. In all fairness may I say that those reform measures are not being received very cordially by the people throughout the country. At least after giving them serious consideration the people are not very enthusiastic about them. According to a biography of the Prime Minister which I read only a short time ago I believe he is the type of man who undoubtedly attended Sunday School in his early years, and for that reason must be conversant with the bible. When they were starting out on a great reform program which was to replace the order that has been in existence for three or four centuries they should have gone back to Holy Writ and endeavoured to obtain some assistance therefrom. From that book they should have taken a guide which could have been followed in forming their reform legislation. Why did they not take a lesson from the life of Jacob, for example? We read that at one time Jacob was travelling from Beer-sheba to Haran-and by the way, he travelled by aeroplane, and that was about five thousand years ago. I say that because the good old book tells us that he landed on a .certain place, and for that reason I judge he must have travelled by plane. Anyway, we learn that after the setting of the sun he landed on this certain place, and being very tired prepared for himself a bed. He took a few stones, placed them together, used them as a pillow, went to sleep and had a dream. He dreamed he saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven. This was not a ladder reaching from earth only part way to heaven; that would have been a mockery. That would have been inadequate-it was a ladder reaching all the way from earth to heaven. I submit that if hon. members of the government when framing this legislation had considered the dream of Jacob their reform measures would have been entirely different and would be adequate to meet existing conditions. Were that the fact the results of the reforms introduced would reach beyond this chamber and into the cottages of the men in distress and those people for whom the reform mea-

_____Long Adjournment-Mr. MacMillan (Mackenzie)
sures are being placed on our statute books.
At the outset may I say that the policies and platform of the Liberal party are always fresh and up to date. It is the only party in Canada to-day in a position to meet the requirements of the hour and the demands of the future. Even if elected, is the party in the corner of the chamber in a position to alleviate the existing distress? Is it in a position to place on the statute books of Canada legislation which would be sufficiently effective? I submit they are not in that position. In the year 1932 the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation came into existence. It had its birth in the city of Calgary in the last days of August, 1932. While in session over a period of two or three days they framed a platform, and I must say that for a period of time I had sympathy with that platform.

speechtext:
Yes, I
had sympathy. I am sympathetic towards everything, but that does not mean that I will support everything. I am sympathetic towards the man who is lost spiritually, politically and otherwise. The platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation received a great deal of consideration and thought in western Canada. I know it did in that portion of Saskatchewan from which I come. The fundamental difference between the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as it originated in Calgary, and the platform of the Liberal party was the stand taken on the land policy, many parts of our platforms were in common, and it would be impossible to have conditions otherwise. The Liberal party has much in common with the Conservative party; that is inevitable. On land matters, however, platforms of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the Liberal party are not in common; in fact that was the fundamental difference between those two parties. It is not necessary for me to elaborate on their land policy, for every member of the house knows as much about it as I do. They were going to give assistance to people who were in debt; those people in return were to transfer their land to the government if the party attained office, and the owners were to become tenants. Now suppose such a thing were to happen that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation should come into office as the federal government of Canada and put their land policy into operation; what, effect would it have upon the people? The great Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose name has gone down to imperishable renown, speaking in the city of Montreal fifty years 92582-164$
ago, said that property rights and property possession were the most sacred things belonging to the individual. But would it remain that way if this policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation were to become operative? I submit that it would not. To become a tenant I submit that a man would have to surrender entirely his spirit of independence. We are not unmindful of the sad and bitter experience of the first tenant known to us in history, that of the Adams' in the garden of Eden. Because of one single violation by one of the tenants of one of the covenants in the lease, the whole family was expelled from the garden. I sometimes think that there must have been a cooperative commonwealth federation group in existence at that time and that it was the leader of the group who found his way into the garden and beguiled the tenant.
If the policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation were carried out, we would lose all property rights. I have here an article which contains an extract from Morgan's Ancient History, as follows;
The idea of property was slowly formed in the human mind, remaining nascent and feeble through immense periods of time. Springing into life in savagery, it required all the experience of this period and the subsequent period of barbarism to develop the germ, and prepare the human brain for the acceptance of its controlling influence. Its dominance as a passion over all other passions marks the commencement of civilization. It not only led mankind to overcome the obstacles that delayed civilization, but to establish political society on the basis of territory and of property. A critical knowledge of the evolution of the idea of property would embody, in some respects, the most remarkable portion of the mental history of mankind.
Independently of the movement which culminated in the patriarchial family of the Hebrew and Latin types, property, as it increased in variety and amount, exercised a steady and constantly augmenting influence ir the direction of monogamy. It is impossible to overestimate the influence of property in the civilization of mankind.
The growth of the idea of property in the human mind commenced in feebleness and ended in becoming its master passion. Government and law's are instituted with primary reference to its creatioh, protection and enjoyment.
The growth of property is thus closely connected with the increase of inventions and discoveries, and with the improvement of social institutions which mark the several ethnical periods of human progress.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if that land plank in the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party were to become operative in this country, before the present generation would pass away we would be reduced to the condition of the nomadic wanderers, upon the primeval plains.

Strange and devious are the paths of history. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had to pass through the fiery furnace of affliction, and during the year 1933, as I have already mentioned, they fought strongly in the constituency of Mackenzie. It was their best fighting ground, and they met with defeat. Then in the provincial elections in Saskatchewan on the nineteenth of June last they were practically put out of business, only five being elected out of fifty-five, and four of them by minority votes. They began to see that they were human like everybody else. They were very anxious to attain office.
Then what happened? At their convention held in the city of Regina in the year 1933 many of the farmers were opposed to nationalizing the land. The farmers were in favour of nationalizing the banks and every other enterprise except themselves. They expressed themselves very strongly in the matter, and I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis),who was an active participant in that convention, lost his temper. I am only surmising that, but when I read the statement that he did make I cannot imagine that it would be made under any ' other conditions than that his mind was agitated and that he was not quite normal.
If the farmer wants a cooperative commonwealth in which everything is socialized but himself, he had better have a cooperative commonwealth of his own.
I would not make that statement unless I was somewhat agitated-offended. He went on to say:
If the farmer is anxious to benefit from the cooperative movement he will have to come half way.
I do not know what is meant by "half way," whether he meant that the farmer should allow half of his possessions to be nationalized and the other half not, but that was the statement of the hon. gentleman, and I admire him for the ground he took; he was sincere. He was espousing principles and policies in which he believed and he wanted to stand his ground. He had said:
If the farmer wants a cooperative commonwealth in wliioh everything is socialized but himself, he had better have a cooperative commonwealth of his own.
He was quite right. When fate was deciding against the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, when they were losing all their elections, they had a convention in the city of Winnipeg last July, and I just want to show you, Mr. Speaker how the influence of that party has dwindled. At every convention they have a group photograph taken; it is the most important business of their convention. I have here the photograph that was taken of the group in the city of Regina. They sat there on July 10, 20 and 21, 1933. I do not know on which of these three days the photograph was taken, but it was the day on which they all looked their best. I have counted the number in the photograph and I find that there are 198, so altogether there must have been 199 persons in the group, because I know that the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) made it his boast in this house last session that he attended that conference. I cannot see his physiognomy in that group, and what happened I think was this; that when the photographer was adjusting his camera my hon. friend from Weyburn started talking about sound money and somebody sat on him. Mind you, there were 1,98 people present. Subsequently the party met in the city of Winnipeg on the seventeenth of July last. Of course they had their photograph taken there also, and would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, there are only eighteen in the group; the number had dwindled in one year from 198 to 18. Of course, we have to allow a certain latitude because the city of Regina is not very attractive compared with Winnipeg, and no doubt in Winnipeg some of them were out taking in the sights. But regardless of attractions in the city of Winnipeg the fact remains that in Regina in 1933 there were 198 present in the group and a year subsequently in Winnipeg there were only 18. Compare that with what took place in the Chateau Laurier on the twentieth of last month. On that evening nearly a thousand souls met to pledge their loyalty and devotion to the Liberal chief. It can easily be seen which party is in the best position to administer the affairs of this country and to satisfy all the electors. There is only one party, the Liberal party. I am not taking the present Conservative government into consideration at all because for the last two or three years the people have decided that they are out or will be out as soon as they have the opportunity to put them out.
I should like to return to a discussion of the human element to which I referred a short time ago. These people have a very human weakness, they are anxious to get into office. As I said before, the fundamental difference between the two parties is the land policy. What happened last year at Winnipeg? They came to the conclusion that they were pursuing the wrong policy and they

Mr. Hyman, a non-voting member of the convention but a member of the provincial legislature, declared that the plank, in its drafted form, was the weakest in the platform. He pointed out in a powerful speech that enemies of the C.C.F. had so worked on the psychology of fear of the farmers by misrepresentation that farmers were afraid of the name. The farmer's land was his most valuable possession and usually it was something he had wrested from nature and developed by the work of his own hands, and he did not want it taken away from him. They all fell for this suggestion, even their leader, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Be is one of the few men in Canada who I think would never veer from a policy he was pursuing once he thought it was right. Subsequently, on December 15, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking in Reston, Manitoba. The people were not yet satisfied; they had grave doubts that if the C.C.F. party was returned to office they would nationalize the land. He stated the aim of the C.C.F. party is to bring about the kingdom of heaven on earth while we are living,-
I concede that, as many of the C.C.F. supporters are saying that this will be a long range program, that it will take many years to be brought into being, and it is quite likely that we will have to be bom again, that we will have to return to our kindred dust when we are reanimated from the tomb to find the C.C.F. at the helm of state. This group claims that they have no connection or association with the communist party of Canada, I believe that that statement is correct, ibut the fact remains that this Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is the best incubator that I know of for the hatching of communist ideas. The three aims for which the two organizations will direct their joint activities are:

Just while I am on that question of salaries, permit me to say that speaking in this house on February 26 last I made mention of the question of salaries and pensions. One of the local papers in the city of Ottawa rather took exception to what I stated then, and attempted to show that I was talking about the civil service superannuation fund. I made no reference whatever, Mr. Speaker, to the superannuation fund, and I do not think we need raise any objection to that because the civil servants pay for their superannuation themselves, and they are entitled to it. Nor did I make any reference to soldiers' pensions. But I did refer to certain other pensions, and I would ask the members of the government to turn to page 22 of the estimates of this year and state whether or not they think that the list of pensions provided in the bottom half of page 22 and on all of page 23, amounting to something over $300,000 a year in payment of pensions to exjudges, is really justified under conditions as they exist in Canada at the present time. The number increases year by year. These pensions run, very many of them, from five, six and seven thousand dollars to as much as twelve thousand dollars a year. I do object to pensions of that kind, and that is what I was referring to. These judges do not pay one dollar while in office to help pay for the pensions which they draw.
There is another thing. This government employs officials, such as the members of the tariff board, at exorbitant salaries, and after they have served a certain number of years they draw pension equal to half of their salary. One of my colleagues mentioned last night the salaries paid to the men in charge of the Bank of Canada. The governor of that bank I believe draws a salary of $30,000, his assistant $20,000, and another assistant $10,000, while the men who do the work are probably drawing from $1,200 to $3,000. That is the thing I object to, and I say that sooner or later this country must come to grips with that problem. This country cannot afford to go on paying pensions at exorbitant rates without receiving something by way of compensation for the donors. It will have to stop.
It is unfair in another respect. I believe there are plenty who do not make that. Then why in the name of heaven should we pay a pension five or six times the amount that these men could earn if they were out in private practice, and give it to them for nothing whatever? It seems to me that if the country were seized of what is going on in that respect they would not stand for it any longer. I intend as long as I can to raise my voice in this house in protest against these pensions.
I do not think that the members of our tariff board, who are engaged at enormous salaries, the chairman at $15,000, and the other two members of the board at $10,000 each- they have nothing to do; they are afraid to

Long Adjournment-Mr. McKenzie
do anything; the only one judgment they handed down that would be of any benefit was appealed by the government and the decision of the board reversed, so they are there for nothing-I do not think they should, after they have served a few years, draw half their salary by way of pension without paying anything towards any pension fund. A few years ago a Liberal government established an annuities branch in the city of Ottawa, and I believe it is a very fine thing. It seems to me that these men who are drawing such enormous salaries should be able to buy their own pensions. By the payment of a few dollars they could provide a pension for themselves, and surely a man who is drawing from eight to thirty thousand dollars a year should be able to pay a few dollars into a pension fund in order to be able to provide a pension for himself.
It is also very unfair to the people who are paying the taxes of this country. I come from a part of the country where there is real hardship. I had a letter today from a lady in one of the towns of my constituency, who said that through the past winter she was drawing $9.50 a month for some work she was doing, taking care of a building in the town, and with that $9.50 a month she kept five of a family off relief. Now when people are existing under such conditions as these, why should they be called upon to pay a cent a pound on all the sugar they consume? Why should they have to pay these high taxes on tea and other necessaries in order to provide pensions of five and six and eight and ten thousand dollars a year to men who neither paid for not earned them? I say that it is very unfair indeed. This government of course will say: Oh, well, that has been going on for years, and it is not only this government that is doing it but other governments have done it as well. I realize that that is true, but conditions at the present time are such that we must not continue to do it any longer.
During the recent budget debate, supporters of the government in their speeches endeavoured in the first place to lay the blame for the loss of trade since 1930 on the previous government. Let us see to what extent that is true. I have here a statement of the trade of Canada with all countries by fiscal years, and I find that in the year 1930 our imports amounted to $1,248,273,000, and our exports in the same year amounted to $1,144,938,000. In 1934 our imports had fallen to $433,776,000, and our exports had fallen to $585,680,000.

When this government came into power our total trade was almost two and a half billion dollars. Now it has fallen below one billion dollars, but this government will try to prove that business had fallen off before they came into power.
Another thing which this government always stresses is that there was a favourable balance of trade of some $115,000,000 during the past year. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think possibly one of the reasons why our imports have fallen down to $433,776,000 is because of the action which this government took in raising the tariff as they did, which prevented goods from entering this country in the first place; and a second reason for the fall in imports is that our working men and our farmers have no income with which to buy the goods even if they were imported. That is why imports fell off to the extent they did. A favourable balance of trade does not mean very much. I would rather have the volume of trade as it was in 1930.
Certain hon. members have made the statement from time to time that Canada has come through the depression better than other countries. I would like that to be true, but when we consider how business has fallen away during the last five years, how revenues have decreased, how debts have increased and how everything possible to be taxed is taxed, how can we say that this country has come through the depression? A week or so ago there appeared in Ottawa a delegation of mayors from cities all the way from Halifax to Vancouver. I should like to repeat some of the statements made at their meetings, which I think are conclusive proof that we are far from being through this depression. It was stated that unemployment relief constitutes a national emergency. It was said that the municipalities are facing bankruptcy and that the country was in the direst distress. These mayors are close to the people and these are some of the expressions which were made at their meetings. They claimed that the depression is not less than it was, it is greater. For the first time the actual facts are now available to hon. me.me,rs. We were told that there would be no want in Canada, but there is want. These men were talking about the conditions in the cities, but how much worse it must be in the rural areas.
I do not think the government of the day has kept its finger upon the pulse of public opinion, especially when such statements as these are made. If this government puts its program into effect and appoints many more boards we will be into bankruptcy much sooner than anticipated.

Long Adjournment-Mr. McKenzie
What does the government expect that people who have not worked eight hours in any day for the last four or five years will think of legislation for an eight hour day or forty-eight- hour week? This matter took up considerable time a few weeks ago, but in my opinion the time is not opportune for such legislation. It might be all right if things were normal, but they are not. Wha-t does a man who has no work care about minimum . wages or maximum hours? All he wants is some work and he is not particular as to the number of hours. I do not think there is much need of this legislation at the present time. I expressed my opinion -of the unemployment insurance measure when it was before the house earlier in the session. I do not think the government- expects that this legislation will be ever put into force, and it will be a good thing for the country if it is not. The Prime Minister has told us that the cost will be between $6,500,000 and $7,000,000 per year.
One measure was passed by this house which I believe will prove to be of some benefit to the community I represent. I refer to the amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. What is going to happen to this legislation? It passed this house over a month ago but it has not passed the senate. Is this house to adjourn for five or six weeks without this legislation receiving royal assent? I receive letters almost every day asking for information in connection with this act. People want to know when they will be able to get money under the provisions of this measure, but I have to tell them that for some reason this bill has not passed through the senate. Perhaps the government could throw some light on the rumour going about to the effect that there is .to be no money made available for the dried out areas of southern Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba.
The government has given as a reason for a five or six week's adjournment that they must prepare legislation made necessary by the report of the price spreads commission. I contend that the government knows at this minute-if it does not know it can find out by inquiring from any daily newspaper in the country-what the legislation is going to be. It is intended that four or five boards will be appointed, and that is all that is to be done. Why not go ahead with the appointment of these boards and let us finish the work of the session and go home to hold an election? That is what the people want.
In conclusion I should like to put on record the particulars in connection with some tariff items which are of considerable concern to
the farming communities of this country. 1 should like to show what has been done in the way of increases in the tariff on agricultural implements. This is a very perplexing question and it will become more so as the years go by. If we have a few crops in the west we will be needing new machinery. Very little machinery has been bought during the last few years and the people have not felt the effect of these higher tariffs on agricultural implements. Some hon. members opposite, particularly those from western Canada, endeavoured to show that there is no difference between the two parties when it comes to tariff matters.

This could be done after we come back from the Easter recess, provided the government still insists on the long recess.
I think this government should also do something about the pensions being paid and for which no contribution is made by the persons receiving them. That is a very sore spot, and I think it is a good thing for governments that the people of the country generally do not know how much is being paid out in this way. It is simply ridiculous and I hope the government will see their way clear to do something about it.
